953.title: Genevieve (3 January)
953.hook: a young woman who calmed Paris during the siege of Attila
953.howItsDone: Catholics keep Saint Genevieve's memory in early January, especially in Paris, where she is honored as the city's patron and people pray for the city in her name.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was litany, and your line was pray for us: a church full of names. Today we start walking the calendar, saint by saint, in January. Day nine hundred fifty-three.

Rumors arrive before armies do. In the story, word reaches Paris that Attila and his Huns are coming, burning cities on the way. People start loading carts. Valuables wrapped in blankets, children on top, the city gates jammed. Neighbors shout advice across the street. Leaving seems like the only sane thing to do. And one young woman stands in the middle of the panic and says: stay. Don't run. Pray. Her name is today's word.
screen: `RUMORS ARRIVE BEFORE ARMIES.` → `CARTS AT THE CITY GATES.` → `ONE VOICE: STAY. PRAY.`

segments.voice: Genevieve lived in Paris in the days when Roman Gaul was coming apart. An early account of her life tells her story, and the Church remembers her in early January. She was a consecrated virgin: not a nun in a convent, but a woman who had given her life to God and lived it out in the city, praying, fasting and caring for people. When the news of Attila came, the account says, she gathered the women of Paris to pray, and she begged the men not to carry their goods away. The cities they fled to, she warned, would not be safe; Paris would be protected. That did not go down well. Some citizens called her a false prophet, and, the account says, they talked about stoning her or throwing her in the river. Then a churchman arrived from Auxerre, where the bishop Germanus had once praised her, and he spoke up for her, and the crowd backed off. And Attila's army turned away. It never reached Paris. Catholics honor Genevieve as the patron of Paris, and her story sits easily next to a line from the Psalms, in the Douay-Rheims: "Unless the Lord keep the city, he watcheth in vain that keepeth it." What she did is ordinary and very hard. She didn't fight. She didn't flee. In a crowd that was spinning, she stayed still, prayed, and asked others to do the same. Calm can be contagious. So can panic. She chose which one to pass on.
screen: `A CONSECRATED WOMAN IN THE CITY.` · `STAY AND PRAY, WHEN EVERYONE RUNS.` · `THE CROWD TURNS ON HER.` · `THE ARMY TURNS AWAY.` · then, large: `UNLESS THE LORD KEEP THE CITY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for your city in a crisis. Settle into the sit and bring your own town to mind. Not the whole map: one street, one hospital, one bus stop. Think of whatever it's facing right now, a storm, a shortage, a fear, a loss. Breathe slowly, the way Genevieve stood still. If you pray, you can ask God to keep your city, or ask Saint Genevieve to pray for it. If you don't, simply hold your city in mind, calmly, without fixing anything. The bell holds the time.
Genevieve. A young woman of Paris who, in the story, urged the city to stay and pray when Attila's army came. Patron of Paris, remembered in early January.
Your line: she calmed the city. Today, when a group chat, a meeting or a kitchen starts to spin, be the slowest, calmest voice in the room once. Day nine hundred fifty-three.

fork.reveal: she gathered the women to pray and begged the men not to leave. the crowd turned on her, a churchman from Auxerre defended her, and the army never reached Paris.

954.title: Kuriakose Elias Chavara (3 January)
954.hook: a Syro-Malabar priest in Kerala who started schools for every parish
954.howItsDone: Syro-Malabar Catholics in Kerala and around the world honor Saint Kuriakose Elias Chavara in early January, especially at Mannanam, where he is buried, and in the schools and religious communities connected with him.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Genevieve, and your line was she calmed the city. Were you the calm voice anywhere? Today, the same day on the calendar, the other side of the world. Day nine hundred fifty-four.

In villages across Kerala, in the south of India, you can still find it: a church, and right next to it, a school. Children in uniforms run between the two at recess. The school bell and the church bell ring from almost the same spot. It looks so natural that nobody asks why. But that pairing didn't happen on its own. Someone asked for it, on purpose, parish by parish. His name is long, and it's today's word.
screen: `A CHURCH IN KERALA.` → `AND RIGHT BESIDE IT, A SCHOOL.` → `SOMEONE ASKED FOR IT, ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: Kuriakose Elias Chavara was a priest of the Syro-Malabar Church, one of the Eastern Catholic Churches, fully Catholic but with its own liturgy and customs. Its people trace their faith back, in their tradition, to the apostle Thomas. Chavara grew up in Kerala, was ordained, and gave his life to renewing that Church from the inside. He helped found a religious congregation of priests and brothers who would pray, preach and teach together. He set up a printing press so books could be made and read at home. He helped start a congregation of religious sisters too. And when he was given authority over the Syro-Malabar parishes, he asked that each parish have a school alongside its church, open to the children of the village. Why a school? Because for him, faith and learning belonged in the same place. A child who could read could read the Gospels, and could also read a contract, a letter, a newspaper. Catholics hear a line of Jesus about children in that work, in the Douay-Rheims: "Suffer the little children, and forbid them not to come to me: for the kingdom of heaven is for such." Chavara also wrote a letter of advice to families, known as the Testament of a Loving Father, full of plain counsel about raising children, keeping the home peaceful and treating servants and neighbors well. Pope Francis declared him a saint. His legacy is easy to walk past: a building with desks, next to a building with an altar.
screen: `A PRIEST OF THE SYRO-MALABAR CHURCH.` · `A CONGREGATION, A PRESS, SISTERS.` · `A SCHOOL BESIDE EVERY CHURCH.` · `ADVICE TO FAMILIES.` · then, large: `SUFFER THE LITTLE CHILDREN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: support a school. Later today, find one small way: a donation of books, an hour of tutoring, a thank-you note to a teacher, a word of encouragement to a child doing homework. For now, settle into the sit. Bring to mind a teacher who changed something for you. See the room, the desk, their face. If you pray, you can pray for them, and for the children in a school near you. If not, simply hold that teacher in mind with gratitude. The bell holds the time.
Kuriakose Elias Chavara. A Syro-Malabar priest in Kerala who founded religious communities, set up a press, and asked for a school beside each parish church. Remembered in early January.
Your line: a school beside every church. Today, put one thing you believe next to one thing you can learn: read a page on a subject you care about. Day nine hundred fifty-four.

what it means: a Syro-Malabar priest who renewed his Church: a congregation, a press, sisters, and a school beside each parish.
what a scholar hears: an Eastern Catholic saint, from a Church that traces its faith to Thomas, whose advice to families is still read.

955.title: André Bessette (early January)
955.hook: a sickly doorkeeper in Montreal who welcomed thousands and built a shrine to Joseph
955.howItsDone: Catholics honor Saint André Bessette in early January; pilgrims visit Saint Joseph's Oratory in Montreal, where he is buried, and some pray there with oil blessed in Saint Joseph's name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kuriakose Elias Chavara, and your line was a school beside every church. What did you read? Today, from Kerala to Canada, and from the classroom to the front door. Day nine hundred fifty-five.

A knock at a school's front door in Montreal. A small, thin man in a religious habit opens it. He takes your coat, asks who you've come to see, and lets you wait by the stove. He does this all day. He sweeps the floor, runs errands, cuts the students' hair. He can barely read. His health was so poor that his religious order nearly sent him away. He later joked that his superiors showed him the door, and he stayed there. That joke, and that man, are today's word.
screen: `A KNOCK AT THE DOOR IN MONTREAL.` → `A THIN MAN TAKES YOUR COAT.` → `THEY SHOWED HIM THE DOOR. HE STAYED.`

segments.voice: André Bessette was a brother of the Congregation of Holy Cross in Quebec. Brother André, people called him. He was weak from childhood, had little schooling, and worked odd jobs before he entered religious life. His community hesitated to keep him, but they did, and they gave him the job of porter, the doorkeeper of their college in Montreal. A doorkeeper sees everyone. Students, parents, the sick, the poor, the curious. André had a deep love for Saint Joseph, the quiet carpenter, and he began to pray with people who came to the door with troubles, especially the sick. He would encourage them to pray to Joseph, and sometimes rubbed them with oil from a lamp burning before Joseph's statue. People said they were healed. Crowds started coming to the door, then to a small wooden chapel he wanted built on the slope of Mount Royal. That chapel grew, over his lifetime and after it, into Saint Joseph's Oratory, a great basilica above the city. André never took the credit. He insisted it was Joseph, and God, who healed; he was only the one who opened the door. There's a psalm line he could have hung over his post, in the Douay-Rheims: "I have chosen to be an abject in the house of my God, rather than to dwell in the tabernacles of sinners." An abject is the lowliest person there. In some translations, it's a doorkeeper. Pope Benedict declared him a saint. The man they nearly sent away is buried in the shrine he started.
screen: `A SICKLY BROTHER, MADE DOORKEEPER.` · `HE PRAYED WITH THE SICK TO JOSEPH.` · `A SMALL CHAPEL GREW INTO AN ORATORY.` · `IT WAS JOSEPH, NOT ME.` · then, large: `I HAVE CHOSEN TO BE AN ABJECT IN THE HOUSE OF MY GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: open the door kindly. Settle in and think of the doors in your day: your front door, an office door, a classroom door, the message you open, the call you pick up. Picture one person who will come through one of them today. See their face before they arrive. If you pray, you can ask Saint Joseph, or Brother André, to pray for them. If not, simply decide in advance to greet them well. The bell holds the time.
André Bessette. Brother André, a frail doorkeeper in Montreal who prayed with the sick to Saint Joseph and began the shrine that became Saint Joseph's Oratory.
Your line: the doorkeeper. Today, hold one door, answer one knock or one message, as if the person on the other side were the most welcome visitor of the day. Day nine hundred fifty-five.

956.title: Marguerite Bourgeoys (12 January)
956.hook: a pioneer teacher in early Montreal, founder of an uncloistered community
956.howItsDone: Catholics remember Saint Marguerite Bourgeoys in January, especially in Montreal and in schools of the Congregation of Notre-Dame, whose sisters still teach and serve without a cloister.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Brother André, and your line was the doorkeeper. Whose knock did you answer well? Today we stay in Montreal, but go back to when it was barely a town. Day nine hundred fifty-six.

A stone stable, empty of animals, swept out. A woman from France stands in it, looking at the walls. Outside is a tiny settlement on an island in a wide river, wooden houses, a fort, forest in every direction, winters she has never imagined. There are only a few children in the whole place. She is going to teach them anyway, here, in this stable. The settlement will become Montreal. The woman is today's word.
screen: `A STONE STABLE, SWEPT OUT.` → `A TINY SETTLEMENT IN THE FOREST.` → `SHE WILL TEACH HERE ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: Marguerite Bourgeoys grew up in Troyes, in France. As a young woman she felt drawn to God, and to teaching, and she joined a group of laywomen who taught poor girls in her town. The governor of the little French settlement of Ville-Marie, on the island that would become Montreal, came looking for a teacher. She crossed the ocean with him. In the settlement she was given a stone stable, and she opened a school in it. But she wanted more than one classroom. She wanted women who would teach wherever they were needed, and that raised a problem. In her day, the Church usually expected women's religious communities to be cloistered: enclosed behind walls, praying, not traveling. Marguerite took her model from Mary in the Gospel of Luke, who, after the angel's visit, went to help her cousin Elizabeth. In the Douay-Rheims: "And Mary rising up in those days, went into the hill country with haste into a city of Juda." A Mary who walked out the door. So her community, the Congregation of Notre-Dame, was uncloistered. Its sisters lived among the people, taught children, trained young women arriving from France to make homes in a hard new place, and went where the need was. Church authorities were cautious at first, and approval took patience. Saint John Paul the Second declared her a saint. She started with a stable and a handful of children. A teacher in the wilderness.
screen: `A LAYWOMAN TEACHER FROM TROYES.` · `A SCHOOL IN A STONE STABLE.` · `MARY WHO SET OUT IN HASTE.` · `SISTERS WITHOUT A CLOISTER.` · then, large: `MARY WENT INTO THE HILL COUNTRY WITH HASTE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: teach someone something. Settle into the sit and think of one thing you know how to do well. A recipe, a shortcut on a phone, a way to fold a shirt, a word in another language, a prayer. Then picture one person who might want to learn it. Later today, offer to show them, simply, the way Marguerite started, with whatever room she had. If you pray, you can ask for patience as a teacher. If not, just hold that person and that small lesson in mind. The bell holds the time.
Marguerite Bourgeoys. A teacher from France who opened a school in a stable in early Montreal and founded the uncloistered Congregation of Notre-Dame. Remembered in January.
Your line: a teacher in the wilderness. Today, in a place where you feel new or out of your depth, share one thing you know with one person there. Day nine hundred fifty-six.

957.title: Hilary of Poitiers (13 January)
957.hook: a married convert who searched his way into the Church, then took exile rather than sign
957.howItsDone: Catholics keep Hilary's memorial in January with the Mass and the Liturgy of the Hours, honoring him as a bishop and Doctor of the Church whose writing on the Trinity is still read.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Marguerite Bourgeoys: a teacher in the wilderness, opening a school in a stable in a town that barely existed yet. Who did you teach something to? Day nine hundred fifty-seven.

A grown man in Roman Gaul, comfortable, educated, with a household of his own, sits with a stack of books and a question that won't leave him alone: what is a human life for? He has tried the philosophers. Eat well, rest well, live decently. It isn't enough. Then he opens the Jewish scriptures and reaches the burning bush, where Moses asks God's name and hears an answer that is barely a name at all. Years later, as a bishop, he will write down that moment of reading as the turn of his life. His name was Hilary, and he would go on to choose exile over a signature. Today, the man who didn't bend.
screen: `WHAT IS A LIFE FOR?` → `THE BURNING BUSH.` → `A BISHOP WHO WOULDN'T SIGN.`

segments.voice: Hilary tells his own story at the start of his book On the Trinity. He says that reading God's words to Moses stopped him. In the Douay-Rheims: "I AM WHO AM." Nothing, he writes, could say more about God than that: God simply is. From there he read on into the Gospels, and asked for baptism. Tradition says he already had a wife and a daughter when he did. Later the people of Poitiers made this married convert their bishop. Then the argument arrived. In Hilary's day, Christians were fighting over whether the Son is truly God, as fully as the Father, or something a step lower. The Emperor favored the bishops who said a step lower, and leaned on the rest to go along, and to condemn Athanasius, the bishop of Alexandria who held that the Son is fully God. Hilary refused. He would not put his name to the condemnation. So he was sent away, far to the east, into exile. And there, cut off from his church, he wrote. On the Trinity starts from the words of baptism, the same closing words of Matthew we heard yesterday, now their second half: "baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." Hilary's point is simple and stubborn. If that is the name you were baptized into, you don't get to quietly edit it later. Eventually he came home to Poitiers and kept teaching. Tradition says a man named Martin, just out of the army, came to learn from him, the man the Church remembers as Martin of Tours. The Church later named Hilary a Doctor of the Church. Steady, here, doesn't mean loud. It means the same answer on a good day and in exile.
screen: `I AM WHO AM: A CONVERT'S TURNING POINT.` · `A MARRIED MAN MADE BISHOP.` · `HE WOULD NOT SIGN, SO HE WAS EXILED.` · `IN EXILE HE WROTE ON THE TRINITY.` · then, large: `IN THE NAME OF THE FATHER, AND OF THE SON, AND OF THE HOLY GHOST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: get ready to defend a friend's name. Settle, and breathe. Hilary wouldn't sign away Athanasius's name when it would have been easy. Bring to mind someone whose name gets handled carelessly when they aren't in the room. A coworker, a sibling, an old friend. Don't rehearse the gossip. Just find one true, good sentence about them that you could say out loud next time. Hold that sentence until it feels steady. If you pray, you can hold that person before God. If you don't, simply keep their face in mind. The bell holds the time.
Hilary of Poitiers. A convert, a married man made bishop, who chose exile over condemning a fellow bishop, and wrote On the Trinity far from home.
Your line: hilary the steady. Today, when someone's name comes up and the room tilts against them, say your one true sentence. Day nine hundred fifty-seven.

958.title: Anthony the Abbot (17 January)
958.hook: the desert father who heard one Gospel line and walked out; patron of animals, blessed in villages on his day
958.howItsDone: Catholics keep Saint Anthony the Abbot's memorial in January, and in some places priests bless farm animals and pets on or near his feast.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hilary of Poitiers, who chose exile over putting his name to a fellow bishop's condemnation. Your line was hilary the steady. Did you get a chance to say your one true sentence? Day nine hundred fifty-eight.

Two graves are fresh in an Egyptian village, and the young man who buried them was their son. He has land, a younger sister to look after, and a lot on his mind. One day he walks into church while the Gospel is being read, and the line being read, his biographer says, landed on him as if it had been read for him alone. He walked out of that church and started giving his fields away. In some villages, on his feast in January, people still bring cows, horses, dogs and chickens to be blessed in his name. Today, the man from the desert, and how a farmyard ended up on his day.
screen: `A YOUNG MAN, NEWLY ORPHANED.` → `ONE GOSPEL LINE.` → `HE GIVES HIS FIELDS AWAY.`

segments.voice: Anthony's story comes to us through the Life of Antony, written by Athanasius, the bishop of Alexandria we met yesterday. The line Anthony heard was Jesus speaking to the rich young man in Matthew's Gospel. In the Douay-Rheims: "If thou wilt be perfect, go sell what thou hast, and give to the poor". Anthony did it. He kept a little back for his sister, Athanasius says, until he heard another Gospel line, about not being anxious for tomorrow, and gave that away too. He placed his sister with a community of faithful women, and went out to live alone. First at the edge of his village, then among old tombs, then deep in the desert, inside an abandoned fort. He stayed there a long time. Athanasius describes the struggle as a real fight: temptations, fear, nights when he felt attacked. And then the surprising part. People came looking for him. When he finally walked out, Athanasius says, his friends were amazed: he looked neither wasted nor overfed, and his mind was calm. Others moved into the desert near him to live the same way, and he taught them. That's why tradition calls him the father of monks. Now the animals. Athanasius tells a small story: wild beasts kept trampling the little garden Anthony grew. He caught one gently and told them all, in effect, I do you no harm, so do me none, and leave. And they left. In time, Christians came to call on him as a patron of animals and farm creatures. So on his day, a priest with holy water in a village square, and a line of farm animals waiting their turn.
screen: `ONE LINE: GO SELL WHAT THOU HAST.` · `ALONE: TOMBS, THEN AN OLD FORT.` · `PEOPLE FOLLOW HIM INTO THE DESERT.` · `THE ANIMALS AND THE GARDEN.` · then, large: `IF THOU WILT BE PERFECT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: care for an animal. Settle, and breathe. If there's an animal near you, a dog, a cat, a bird at the window, give it your full attention for a while. Notice how it breathes. If there isn't one, bring to mind an animal you've loved, or one you saw today. Then decide one small kindness: fresh water, a walk that's longer than usual, a little food for the birds. If you pray, you can give thanks for that creature. If you don't, just let it be good that it exists. The bell holds the time.
Anthony the Abbot. The Egyptian who heard one Gospel line, gave his land away, and went to the desert. Others followed, and he became the one tradition calls the father of monks.
Your line: the father of monks. Today, do the small kindness for an animal that you chose, and notice how little it takes. Day nine hundred fifty-eight.

959.title: Sebastian (20 January)
959.hook: a soldier-martyr painted pierced with arrows, who in his story survives them; patron of athletes
959.howItsDone: Catholics keep Saint Sebastian's memorial in January, and sports clubs, athletes and soldiers in various places honor him as a patron.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Anthony the Abbot, who heard one Gospel line and walked into the desert. Your line was the father of monks. What kindness did an animal get from you? Day nine hundred fifty-nine.

In a gallery of old paintings, a young man looks back at you, tied to a tree or a column, calm, with arrows standing out of his body. It's easy to assume you're looking at the moment he died. In his story, they aren't. The arrows are the part he survived. His name is Sebastian, and today ends a week of saints from the calendar's first weeks of January. Today, the soldier, and what happened after the arrows.
screen: `A YOUNG MAN AND THE ARROWS.` → `NOT THE MOMENT HE DIED.` → `WHAT CAME AFTER.`

segments.voice: Very little about Sebastian is certain. Saint Ambrose, the bishop of Milan, mentions him as a martyr from Milan who died in Rome. The full story comes from a much later account of his martyrdom. Here is the story it tells, the one the Church has handed down. Sebastian was an officer in the emperor's guard and a Christian, quietly. He used his post to visit Christians in prison and to keep their courage up. When he was found out, the emperor had him tied up and shot with arrows by his own fellow soldiers, and left for dead. A Christian widow named Irene came at night to take his body for burial, and found him breathing. She took him home and nursed him. And here's the turn. Healed, Sebastian did not leave Rome. He went and stood where the emperor would pass, and told him to his face that he was wrong to persecute Christians. This time he was beaten to death. So the arrows didn't stop him. Tradition honors him as a patron of athletes and soldiers, and some readers see why: a body that took the blow and got back up. Some readers hear in him the words Paul writes near the end of his second letter to Timothy. In the Douay-Rheims: "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith." A fight, a race, a finish line. Look back at this week's calendar and you'll see a whole team: Genevieve calming Paris, Kuriakose Chavara putting a school beside a church, André the doorkeeper, Marguerite teaching in a stable, Hilary refusing to sign, Anthony walking into the desert. And Sebastian, getting back up.
screen: `A REAL MARTYR, A LATER LEGEND.` · `A SOLDIER WHO VISITED PRISONERS.` · `IRENE FINDS HIM BREATHING.` · `HE GOES BACK TO THE EMPEROR.` · then, large: `I HAVE FINISHED MY COURSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for athletes. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who trains their body. A kid at Saturday soccer, a friend who runs before work, a player on a team you follow, someone learning to walk again after an injury. Picture them in the hard part, the last stretch, the moment they want to stop. If you pray, you can ask Sebastian to pray for them. If you don't, wish them strength and a safe body, one name at a time. The bell holds the time.
Sebastian. A soldier-martyr of Rome. In his story he survived the arrows, was nursed by Irene, and went back to face the emperor.
Your line: arrows didn't stop him. Today, when something knocks you flat, take one small step of getting back up, and notice who helped you, the way Irene helped him. Day nine hundred fifty-nine.

fork.setup: you're Sebastian. you survived the arrows and Irene has nursed you back to health. the emperor thinks you're dead. what do you do?
options: slip out of Rome and live quietly somewhere else.
stay hidden in Irene's house.
go and stand where the emperor will pass.
fork.reveal: in the story he confronted the emperor about persecuting Christians, and was beaten to death.

original.note: Latin: his name as the Roman calendar keeps it.

trapdoor: what you thought: the saint who died full of arrows.
what it means: in his story the arrows don't kill him. Irene nurses him, and he goes back to face the emperor.
what a scholar hears: Ambrose names a martyr Sebastian of Milan; the detailed story of the arrows and Irene comes from a much later account.
